LEU025X10.name: French Basic 2 (B1)
LEU025X10.content:
This module aims at developing the skills of expressing your opinion in a structured way, as well as defending and illustrating your positions in French.
Please note that the language course units offered by ELC are more than straightforward proficiency courses. You can expect to work actively on your general language proficiency as well as your cultural knowledgeabout the French speaking world, language, literature and politics. To do so, you will engage in tasks and activities with authentic journalistic, administrative and academic content.
LEU025X10.entry: French Basic 1 or French Basic 1b must be completed successfully.

LEU067P10.name: French Basic 1 (A2)
LEU067P10.content:
This module aims at developing the skills of expressing yourself simply and correctly on everyday topics. It also aims at explaining your choices in French.
Please note that the language course units offered by ELC are more than straightforward proficiency courses. You can expect to work actively on your general language proficiency as well as your cultural knowledge about the French speaking world, language, literature and politics. To do so, you will engage in tasks and activities with authentic journalistic, administrative and academic content.

LFW003B10.name: Global Change: Contemporary Issues
LFW003B10.content:
To prepare students for job recruitments and problem-oriented professional assignments, this ourse teaches how to approach complex problems and work towards potential solutions. It introduces students to the concept of “wicked problems”. These are planning and social policy
problems that defy simple or final solutions, because of their complexity, interconnectedness and conflicting stakeholder perspectives. They can at best be tamed, not solved. In particular, the course discusses interconnected national and international dynamics, social and
technological components of problems, involved private and public actors, and strategies to reconcile conflicting societal interests and values. In the course of ten thematic lectures and ten tutorial sessions, students learn to leverage their disciplinary background to make a
contribution to solving a wicked problem in small interdisciplinary teams. The course starts off with an evaluative introduction to the “wicked problem” approach and then proceeds to in-depth discussions of a range of current global challenges including inequalities within and between
societies, ecological transformations, migration, AI, health, resilience, and global governance.
LFW003B10.entry:
This module is open for:
This module is open for: 
- students with a positive BSA from all BA programmes at the Faculty of Arts (*)
(*) The following BA programmes do not take part in 2026-2027:
Dutch Languages and Cultures; History; Linguistics.

LFW003P10.name: Global Change: Global Change in Context
LFW003P10.content: In this course, students identify major contemporary global challenges in their historical context and learn to analyse them through multidisciplinary perspectives. Concretely, the course asks whether the established narrative of an ever more integrated world is still suitable to explain our present experiences in various fields including the economy, politics, culture, ecology and social relations. Starting off with a more in-depth discussion on what we mean by globalisation, the course expands on a number of key transformations that alter societies around the world as well as international relations. This includes ideological advocates and opponents of globalization, economic (dis)integration, political globalisation and conflict, cultural hybridisation and homogenisation, ecological disruption, changing patterns of mobility and communication, and social connectivity and distancing. The course combines sources, frameworks, and interpretations from various academic cultures and regions around the globe.
LFW003P10.entry:
This module is open for:
* students of the BA European Languages and Cultures
* students of the BA History
* students of the BA International Relations and International Organization
* students of the BA Middle Eastern Studies
* exchange students at the Faculty of Arts

LYX001B10.name: Policy & Governance
LYX001B10.content:
Policy and Governance highlights the relationship between state or EU level and society. Throughout the course, concepts such as ‘governance,’ ‘democratic stability,’ ‘electoral processes,’ ‘elections,’ ‘interest representation,’ ‘bureaucracy,’ ‘policy implementation’ and many others are discussed both from a theoretical and comparative perspective. As such, the course unravels the essence of the state and is constantly juxtaposing this with the policy processes that can be identified as taking place at the European Union level. 

Besides testing the students’ knowledge of the material discussed in the lectures and seminars, the students will participate in a simulation meeting of the EU’s European Council and Council of Ministers to apply their theoretical knowledge in practice.
LYX001B10.entry: Admittance to the second year IRIO. Exchange Students must have completed at least 45 ECTS of a relevant major in International Relations or International Politics.

LYX030P10.name: Introduction to International Relations
LYX030P10.content:
This course provides an introduction to the main skills and concepts  to understand to study International Relations at university. The course introduces you to major concepts in the discipline of International Relations and discusses these in lectures as well as small-group tutorial settings.

You will also receive a solid grounding in how international relations can be approached as a social science, how to think about some of the big questions that you might have as you start your degree programme, and some of the skills that you will need to conduct independent academic research on subjects of your choice.

The course consists of two complementary parts, with the first part focusing on how to approach the study of IR practically and theoretically, while the second part applies those skills to specific concepts.

This all provides a solid foundation for future courses such as Analysing International Relations, Global Change, Methodology and Research Practice, and your eventual BA thesis as well as future studies.
LYX030P10.entry: Admittance to the BA IRIO. Available to exchange students of Arts.

LYX031P05.name: Historical Foundations of Modern IR
LYX031P05.content: Historical Foundations of Modern IR addresses the history of international relations and international thought in the long nineteenth century from a global perspective. Students will acquire a basic understanding of the historical processes and ideas driving global transformations, in order to provide the historical context necessary to understand contemporary global affairs. Specifically, the course unit covers the topics of great power politics, imperialism, and industrialization as core nineteenth century dynamics, and the traditions of liberalism, nationalism, and socialism as ideological underpinnings of both nineteenth century and contemporary politics. The impact of these dynamics and ideologies will be examined in both European and non-European contexts.
LYX031P05.entry: Admittance to the BA IRIO. Available to exchange students of Arts.

LYX032P05.name: Economics for Public Policy
LYX032P05.content:
Economics for Public Policy introduces students to how a modern economy functions within an internationally interdependent environment. We will cover introductory material in both microeconomics and macroeconomics, with an emphasis on the consequences of policy choices (e.g., taxation, spending, market regulation, trade policy, redistribution). Students will be encouraged to approach these problems from an international political economy perspective, considering how political power can affect the operation of markets and vice versa. This material will form the foundation for students’ further studies of global political economy.

The course will be assessed with a written exam with some digital elements.
LYX032P05.entry: Admittance to the BA IRIO. Available to exchange students of Arts.

LYX033P05.name: Contemporary Global History
LYX033P05.content: The course unit Contemporary Global History form a composite whole with its predecessor, Historical Foundations of Modern IR. It addresses the development of international relations in the twentieth and early 21st centuries, where both are understood as interwoven historical processes and contemporary global affairs. Specifically, the course highlights connectivities between Western and Non-Western perspectives on phenomena such as nation-state formation or the development of an international order. Concrete examples are provided throughout the course
LYX033P05.entry: Admittance to the BA IRIO. Available to exchange students of Arts.

LYX034P05.name: Political Systems in the World
LYX034P05.content:
Political Systems in the World introduces students to mainstream political science with a strong comparative focus. The course explores the tools and methods of comparative analysis, foundational concepts (e.g., democracy, autocracy, and political culture), and key institutions (e.g., electoral systems and parties). It also addresses contemporary challenges such as democratic backsliding, populism, and immigration politics, with a focus on regions beyond Europe and the United States. Throughout the course, we will move beyond a simple description of foreign countries to explore the underlying structures of power. By the end of the course, students will be able to move from asking “what happened?” to “why did it happen here and not there?”

The course combines lectures and tutorials: 
- Lectures outline the study material and clarify the relationships between its components
- Tutorials provide students with the opportunity to apply their theoretical knowledge by analyzing and critiquing assigned readings
LYX034P05.entry: Admittance to the BA IRIO. Available to exchange students of Arts.

LYX035P10.name: Analysing International Relations
LYX035P10.content:
You have enrolled in a degree of International Relations, so you now have a problem! People will expect you to analyse problems related to order, power, and governance across the globe, in an authoritative manner. As you will have experienced, this is not simple and will demand from you the capacity to think independently and creatively, not just to spell-out what others have said. This course is designed to help you start doing it. 

Because analysis is not a matter of employing analytical perspectives as templates, or about finding the right information to be able to answer ready-made questions, you must develop your capacity to be creative and resourceful when engaging with any matter of international relations. Sometimes we do not need too much information to learn about something. We just need to pose the right kind of questions and use our material creatively. 

In academia we combine reflexive knowledge (theories and perspectives) with analytical experience (empirical analysis). In your first semester you begun to acquire the former. We will now help you develop the latter. This means that we will be drawing on what you already know about international relations to use it in the analysis of real-life cases. We will of course expand our theoretical knowledge but we will emphasise the use of knowledge to make sense of phenomena. The creative aspect comes by using the knowledge resources at our disposal to create our own interpretations based on solid arguments and evidence.  

This course is built around an experiential pedagogy that will help you learn, through your own life-experience, about how the world is and has been order(ed), how power works, and how does governance take place in the world. We will reflect on them through a series of tailored-made lectures (in the first block), and seminars (on the second block) that will demand from you continuous reading about world affairs, specialist texts, and collective discussions. Because of this approach, we will not be following a textbook but employing published academic articles and book sections.

LYX076B10.name: Methodology and Research Practice
LYX076B10.content: MRP provides students with a practical lecture-seminar learning environment in which students will be introduced to the practice of inquiry and research methods in International Relations. The lecture portion of this module will introduce students to methodological debates within the social sciences, research design, and research operationalization. Students will have the option to specialize in two principal seminar streams, interpretive research and international public policy, exploring a variety of methodological approaches and practical applications. The seminars will take the form of intensive methods workshops in which students will be expected to carry out research projects and communicate their research findings in a range of formats that include: policy briefs and research essays. MRP aims to give students a strong foundation in applied research methods and skills that are transferable across a wide range of research careers.
LYX076B10.entry: Admittance to the second year IRIO.

LYX104B10.name: Theory of International Relations
LYX104B10.content: The module offers an introduction to the most important schools and approaches within International Relations (IR) theory, as well as to broad epistemological debates. The analytical use of theory and the relationship between theory and practice will be dealt with. The module makes use of weekly (plenary) lectures, in which theories are presented in a textbook-like manner, and accompanying weekly (small-group) seminars, in which through selected readings conceptual, logical and empirical/normative merits of each approach will be discussed and paper instruction (research, writing) is provided. Seminar attendance is mandatory. Assessment for this course is based on written and oral assessment, and a larger end-of-term research paper - all on a theoretical topic and delivering a theoretical analysis and argument.
LYX104B10.entry: Admittance to the second year IRIO.

LYX168B10.name: International Law and Organizations
LYX168B10.content: The course International Law and International Organizations offers a broad perspective on the history and current state of international law. lt looks specifically into the content of international legal norms and the structure and performance of international organizations with an emphasis on international courts and the United Nations system. The course is designed for International Relations students in that it emphasizes the power relations and the historical dynamics behind international legal systems, law-making processes of regional and global reach, and state compliance and responsibility vis-a-vis key international regimes such as human rights, international criminal law, humanitarian law, trade or environmental law, among others. The course aims to develop 'legal literacy' for International Relations students by exploring how global politics are translated into international law and how international law, in turn, shapes global politics.
LYX168B10.entry: Admittance to the second year of BA IRIO. Available to exchange students of Arts.

LYX169B05.name: Global Political Economy
LYX169B05.content: A widely held misconception is that global issues are either political or economic in nature. With their separate discussions of business and politics media commentary encourage such divisions. This course challenges the separation of global politics and international economics. It explores economic aspects of politics and political aspects of economics within and beyond nation-states. The field of Global Political Economy is presented as distinct from International Economics. Students will explore several analytical approaches to understanding key structures and issues in the contemporary global political economy.
LYX169B05.entry: Admittance to the second year of BA IRIO. For exchange students of Arts: Basic knowledge of Economics is required.

LYX170B05.name: IR Today
LYX170B05.content: From the conflicts in the Middle East, Europe, Africa and elsewhere, to the purported end of the international liberal order (ILO) and shifting power centres in the global economy, to ongoing structural challenges facing societies globally —including those linked with climate change, inequality, and populism—international relations is at the forefront of daily life and public attention. It is the task of International Relations (IR) as an academic discipline to build theoretical and empirical insights into these events and trends. Hence, this course centres on examining contemporary issues in international relations by drawing on cutting-edge scholarly insights across the diverse range of IR’s sub-fields and associated disciplines, including security, political economy, law and governance, political theory, among others.
LYX170B05.entry: Admittance to the second year of BA IRIO. Available to exchange students of Arts.

LYX182B10.name: SM: Geopolitics and International Law
LYX182B10.content:
While often treated as two separate, and even opposing, practices and fields of global politics, this course seeks to understand the interplay between geopolitics and international law. For this it introduces different approaches and analytical tools to understand the relationship between
international law and geopolitics, and links this to historical and current international dynamics. In a first step, we will familiarize ourselves with current debates in the academic fields of geopolitics and the politics of international law and try to bring these often-separate fields together by asking, for example, whether international law operates as an instrument of power politics or actually tames these dynamics. We will discuss in this context also the limits and possibilities of interdisciplinary research as well as develop a conceptual vocabulary to investigate projects in the intersection of international law and geopolitics. We will then, in a second step, turn to a variety of historical and current examples like the use of extraterritorial jurisdiction by European powers in China, Japan and the Ottoman Empire during the nineteenth century; the emergence of ‘lawfare’ in the context of the debate on humanitarian
interventions in the 1990s; the legal landscape of war in particular after the Russian invasion in Ukraine; and the judicio-political infrastructure of current geo-economic projects.
LYX182B10.entry: Students must have obtained the first year of the degree programme. In the second year of the Bachelor, 20 ECTS must have been obtained in non-language modules, as well as MRP. Exchange students of Arts must have completed at least 45 ECTS of a relevant major in International Relations or International Politics.

LYX999B10.name: Bachelor's Thesis IRIO
LYX999B10.content: The BA-thesis is related to the Specialization Module IRIO. The BA-thesis presents a reasoned argument based on the student’s own analysis, dealing with a topic that is of relevance to one of the themes of the bachelor’s degree programme, such as Global Governance, International Political Economy, European Integration, and International Security. The bachelor’s thesis is the result of a substantial study of literature and sources, and should demonstrate the use of international relations theoretical and methodological frameworks, techniques or approaches.
LYX999B10.entry: Specialization Module must be passed in order to start the thesis.
